hierarchy

/HY-rar-kee/ — stress on first syllable · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A hierarchy is a system that ranks people or things by level of importance or authority, from the highest down to the lowest.

In the office hierarchy, interns report to analysts, and analysts to managers.

Example

The marine captain read the command hierarchy before the mission: sailors reported to petty officers, petty officers to lieutenants, and lieutenants to the captain.

Hierarchy is more precise than 'chain of command' or 'pecking order' because it emphasizes the entire structure of authority ranked from top to bottom. The word captures the complete system of authority, not just that some people rank higher than others.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

ladder: A ladder is a figurative series of ranked levels for one person to climb — you picture someone rising rung by rung toward the top. A hierarchy is not about anyone's climb: it names the whole fixed structure of levels itself, from the lowest rank to the highest.

chain of command: A chain of command is the official order of who answers to whom — one straight line of authority running from a private up to a general. A hierarchy is bigger than any one line: it names the entire ranked system, every level and every branch at once.

pecking order: A pecking order is an informal, unspoken ranking that a group works out on its own — nobody writes it down or announces it. A hierarchy is the opposite in exactly that way: a formal, openly stated system that fixes people or things into exact levels.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

equality: everyone holding exactly the same rank

anarchy: absence of any authority or ranking system

Where it sits · how strictly rank is layered — shared authority → loose roles → clear reporting lines → hierarchy

shared authority vs. hierarchy: With shared authority, no one outranks anyone else — the opposite end of the scale from a hierarchy.

loose roles vs. hierarchy: Loose roles hint at who does what without ranking anyone, while a hierarchy fixes people into exact levels.

clear reporting lines vs. hierarchy: Clear reporting lines show who answers to whom, and a full hierarchy stacks those lines into a complete top-to-bottom system of rank.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — hier-

Root — hier-: sacred, holy (Greek (hieros))

Root — arch

Root — arch: rule, ruler, leader (Greek (arkhos, arkhein))

Suffix — -y

Suffix — -y: state, condition, or system of (Greek (-ia))

Put it together

Put it together: Hierarchy is literally 'rule by the sacred' — the original hierarchies ranked priests from the highest order down to the lowest. English kept the top-to-bottom ranking system and let go of the religious meaning.

Use the root in a new word: monarchy

Use the root in a new word: monarchy: The little country stayed a monarchy long after its neighbors had written republican constitutions — the same arch root that ranks a hierarchy's levels.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / neutral

Hierarchy is the word when you need to name a system of authority or ranking—think organizational charts, military chains, or social structures. For a simple statement that one person is 'above' another, plain words like 'the parents decide more' work better. Reach for hierarchy when the structure itself is important.
